title: Against the convenient city
gist: Engelsberg Ideas' deputy editor argues that app-enabled e-bike networks and takeaway delivery — Lime bikes, the near-silent rider swarms of central Glasgow — have done as much as anything in the last decade to fragment the incidental social contact that makes cities work, producing a hollowed-out version of the Hansa and 19th-century civic ideal. He concedes the convenience is genuinely valuable (medicine and food for the bedbound) but frames the class split as: who orders the Vietnamese, and who rides it over.

insights.claim: The spread of e-bike networks and the rise in mobile-technology-enabled delivery riders have done as much as anything in the last decade to fragment the connections on which a day-to-day civic sensibility depends.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Names a social externality of the on-demand economy that is not yet priced by regulators or platforms — the likely basis for future municipal restrictions on micromobility and delivery.
insights.locator: Among the essential innovations in urban life

insights.claim: The convenient version of urban society perfected in the last few years is a hollowed-out version of older dreams of city life, because the burghers of the Hansa towns, the Italian city-states and Britain's great 19th-century cities also believed in money, convenience and speed but built cities that were thoroughly peopled and noisy.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Separates commercial dynamism from frictionlessness — historically the two coexisted with density, so the current trade-off is a choice, not an inevitability.
insights.locator: The convenient version of urban society

insights.claim: When reforming mayor Joseph Chamberlain drove a vast thoroughfare through Birmingham's inner-city slums he wanted it full of people shopping and pursuing daily urban opportunities — a deliberate design for density rather than throughput.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: A historical benchmark for evaluating current urban redevelopment: whether the design target is footfall or frictionless transit.
insights.locator: When reforming mayor of Birmingham Joseph Chamberlain

insights.claim: The author's core claim is that living in cities means rubbing along, sometimes uncomfortably, with thousands of people you will never speak to, that the rubbing along is the point, and that avoiding it amounts to the dream of suburbia.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: If a city optimised for convenience converges functionally on suburbia, the premium paid for urban property is buying something the convenience economy is actively eroding.
insights.quote: But the rubbing along is part of the point; avoiding it would require city-dwellers to live somewhere else altogether. And that is the dream of suburbia.
insights.locator: To live in cities is to rub along

insights.claim: Lime bikes are globally identical — a Lime bike in New York is the same as one in London or Paris — and seem designed to be ugly, possibly as a cheap form of advertising, whereas London's Boris bikes and Paris' Vélib' at least carry a concrete local visual identity.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Global fleet standardisation is an operating-cost advantage for the platform and an aesthetic cost borne by the city — a fault line for licensing negotiations.
insights.quote: A Lime bike in New York is the same as one in London or Paris.
insights.locator: The first, e-bikes, are a quicker way

insights.claim: From dinner time into the small hours, streets in cities with high student populations and dense flat blocks become a racecourse for delivery e-bike riders who also flood the pavements — almost silent but very fast — with central Glasgow described as the worst example, where the only crowds are men loitering as they wait for orders.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: A concrete deterrent to city-centre footfall from suburban visitors — directly relevant to high-street retail and hospitality demand in student-dense centres.
insights.quote: The streets – and, shamefully, the pavements, too – are flooded at peak hours with riders, almost silent but very fast.
insights.locator: The marriage of convenience with ugliness

insights.claim: E-bikes deliver real utility — quicker errands, getting home late at night, cycling without arriving drenched in sweat — and the author personally took one home from South London after the England-Norway quarter-final, saving about 20 minutes, yet regretted the silent route over the post-midnight tube.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: The author concedes the product works, locating the objection in what the substitution displaces rather than in the service quality — a harder critique for platforms to answer.

insights.claim: Delivery is not cheap and the convenience can be genuinely helpful, with medicine and food arriving speedily for the ill and bedbound cited as the clearest case of real value.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: The defensible use case for on-demand delivery is accessibility, not discretionary convenience — the framing platforms will need for regulatory legitimacy.
insights.locator: Making time is one of the most significant challenges

themes.theme: Class Structure of the Delivery Economy

insights.claim: The author reframes the delivery economy as a class question — who orders the Vietnamese, who expects it to arrive seamlessly in minutes, and who no longer thinks to walk to the restaurant — placing the rider and the orderer on opposite sides of the same transaction.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: The labour-versus-consumer split inside gig delivery is the political fault line that drives worker-classification regulation and platform cost structures.
insights.quote: This is the other side of the class dynamic of the contemporary city – who orders the Vietnamese?
insights.locator: This is the other side of the class dynamic

insights.claim: Vincenzo Latronico's 2022 satire Perfection is used as the archetype: an Italian couple working as freelance online marketers in Berlin move from early optimism to inertia, never learn German after more than a decade, order in takeaways, work from home in a daily fugue state of endless scrolling, and eventually rent out the apartment to fund elaborate holidays and work from anywhere.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: A portrait of the location-indifferent remote knowledge worker who consumes a city's amenities while contributing nothing to its civic fabric — the demand profile behind short-let and co-living markets.
insights.locator: Vincenzo Latronico’s 2022 satire of Berlin hipsterdom
